newsitem.title: GERMANY: German insurers disagree over intermediaries' bill.
newsitem.headline: German insurers disagree over intermediaries' bill.

text.p: A sharp dispute has arisen in the German insurance industry over plans to introduce a bill covering the qualification of agents and a central register for them, insurance executives said.

In particular, companies with a large number of part-time agents, such as HUK-Coburg or Nuernberger, oppose such a law. They fear that the sale of policies by, for example, car dealers or public servants, will in future be made much more difficult or even impossible.
However, most companies in the insurance federation Gesamtverband der Deutschen Versicherungswirtschaft (GDV) favour such a bill.

The Bonn government has so far not taken the initiative on this issue, it did not transform a European Union directive on intermediaries into German law. But the state of Lower Saxony has now started procedures to introduce legislation via the states' chamber, the Bundesrat.
Mr Rolf-Peter Hoenen, chief executive of low-cost motor insurer HUK-Coburg, told Reuters that he was "strictly against any form of legislation."

Konrad Falk, head of the Nuernberger property and casualty group, said: "This bill, if passed, would mean a massive encroachment on free competition." Its purpose was not to protect the consumer, but to get rid of part-time agents and to hit those insurers which rely on them, he told Reuters.
Falk took the issue to the floor of last week's GDV general meeting in Stuttgart, where he formally protested against the organisation's stance on this issue - a very rare event for GDV.
Germany has about 59,000 full-time and at least 300,000 part-time agents. There is no regulation of this profession, and anybody may sell insurance policies.

The bill now prepared by the state of Lower Saxony seeks a minimum qualification and a register of agents. The GDV majority is in favour of legislation, although unhappy with the detailed wording of the Lower Saxony proposal.

It is seeking to exclude part-time representatives from the regulations. However, should this exclusion not be achieved, the GDV majority says, it would favour a rule that part-time agents must be attached to a full-time (and registered) agent.

Konrad Falk of Nuernberger believes that this 'attachment clause' in particular would be a grave violation of competition rules. Nuernberger group member Garanta, for example, sells motor policies via car dealers, which would be especially hit by such a rule.
Falk believes that any such law would be unconstitutional, adding that Nuernberger would certainly fight it.
